Bui Quang Tuan

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: Drag the corners of a triangle and watch six circles fit into it, one after another.
How to play: Drag A1, A2, A3 or the point P, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Use the buttons to show names or join the circle centres.
Look for the math

Bui Quang Tuan found a surprising loop inside an ordinary triangle. Put one circle in a corner, then fit the next one against it in the next corner, and keep going. After six circles you are back where you started. This is a new twist on an old puzzle of H. Eves.

Six circles that close up

Start with a circle touching the two sides of angle A3-A1-A2. Mark where it touches side A1A2: call that point T12. The second circle is tangent to the first at T12 and sits in the next corner, so it also touches A2A3 at T23. Continue around the corners A3, A1, A2, A3, A1, A2. The article's claim is that the seventh circle is exactly the first: C7 = C1. The logic test checks the centre and the radius of that seventh circle on the starting picture and on 300 other triangles; both come back the same.

The touching points make one circle

The six common points of tangency are concyclic: one circle passes through all six. Even better, its centre is the incenter of the triangle — the point equally far from all three sides. The test measures those distances independently and confirms the claim. The green dashed circle on the picture is this circle of tangency points.

A hexagon made of centres

Join the six circle centres in order. The article says they form a parahexagon: opposite sides are parallel and the same length. Walking round the hexagon, side 1 is the opposite of side 4, side 2 of side 5 and side 3 of side 6; the test compares all three pairs over the same 300 triangles. Press Join centers to see the hexagon.

Try dragging P far along the angle bisector: the circles change size, but the seventh still lands on the first.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
